title: Experiment with further performance improvements of walking with `os.Root`

comments.body:
## Problem

When walking into all subdirectories of a given directory, caching only the most recent entry makes the cache reopen the `os.Root` of the parent directory once for every subdirectory it contains.

Furthermore, when constructing `os.Root`, it uses `openat` to walk every component of a given path.

## Benchmark parameter modification

To make the directory caching more visible in the benchmark, I edited the parameters to generate a tree with more directories.

```diff
diff --git a/storage/internal/rootlookupcache/benchmarks_test.go b/storage/internal/rootlookupcache/benchmarks_test.go
index 560d382bf3..9deaef4b2a 100644
--- a/storage/internal/rootlookupcache/benchmarks_test.go
+++ b/storage/internal/rootlookupcache/benchmarks_test.go
@@ -18,9 +18,9 @@ import (
 // and a potential for improvement.
 
 const (
-       maxDepth      = 4
-       entriesPerDir = 100
-       dirDivider    = 25
+       maxDepth      = 5
+       entriesPerDir = 10
+       dirDivider    = 2
 )
 
 func benchmarkDir(b *testing.B) string {
```

After this modification, the benchmark (which should be perceived as an estimate throughout the document) produced the following results:

| Variant        | Times slower compared to `NoRoot` |
|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| StepByStepWalk | 1.31                              |
| Cached         | 1.87                              |
| Uncached       | 3.24                              |

## Improving caching

I started with trying how far we can get without reimplementing `WalkDir`. The motivation for this would be being able to:

- keep using standard-library-maintained implementation
- limit the opened file descriptor for an arbitrary `n` of directories, counting from the currently deepest one (as with the recursive implementation, the cache we would want to close would be far in a different call on the stack)
- implement custom walking without the additional complexity of including the caching inside, while being able to reuse a single caching implementation between them

### Basic idea

At given time, every subdirectory from the left (such as `["a", "a/b", "a/b/c"]` for `"a/b/c/file"`) has an open `os.Root` in the cache entries. When going deeper, the next `os.Root` gets opened from the previous frame in the cache, that way the `os.Root`s are chained (for example, it is not necessary to walk `"a/b/c/d"`, as it can be accessed as opening `"d"` from the cached root of `a/b/c`) to save the cost of re-walking for opening `os.Root`s.

After this cache modification, benchmark went as follows:

| Variant        | Times slower compared to `NoRoot` |
|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| StepByStepWalk | 1.12 (10% faster)                              |
| Cached         | 1.65 (7.6% faster)                             |
| Uncached       | 3.17                              |

#### Profiling with `pprof`

`Cached`:

```
3.08s 76.62%  io/fs.WalkDir
2.12s 52.74%  io/fs.ReadDir
0.94s 23.38% go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.BenchmarkCached.func1
0.14s 3.48%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.(*Cache).RootForDir
```

Out of the whole walk (76.62%), about 2/3 (52.74%) are caused by `fs.ReadDir`. The closure ran in the benchmark takes roughly the remaining 1/3 (23.38%).

`StepByStepWalk`:

```
2.22s 68.94%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.rootedWalkDirFn
1.02s 31.68%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.rootedWalkDirFn.func1
1.01s 31.37%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.BenchmarkStepByStepWalk.func1
0.13s  4.04%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.(*Cache).RootForDir
```

Less than half (31.68%) of the whole walk (68.94%) is spent on the custom implemented walking. The closure ran in the benchmark takes roughly the same time (31.37%).

#### Profiling conclusion

For this directory-heavy benchmark, I would say it looks like the primary bottleneck is the inefficient implementation of `ReadDir` rather than the limitations of the current cache or the inability to get the handle directly from `fs.WalkDir`.

Before the cache improvement, the code gets 30% improvement mostly by bypassing the `ReadDir` calls. Another 7% then comes from the current improvement, which prevents redundant reopening of roots together with avoiding their repeated walks of `openat` by the chaining.

### Limiting open file descriptors

Having a (or even two) file descriptors for every directory may hit the limit of the process in extreme cases, and even if limit isn't a problem in a particular case, inefficiency still might be.

#### a) Keeping `n` shallowest directories

##### In cache:

The cache would properly work for the `n` directories, and lookup for `n+m` would result in:

```go
frames[n-1].dirRoot.Open("path/without/the/first/n/segments")
```

##### In recursive implementation:

By using the cache outside of the recursion. Otherwise it could be having two recursive implementations: the first would work naturally, the second would have to close file descriptors before the recursive descend, but that is inefficient as after `n` is reached, it gets reduced to the no cache mechanism.

##### Either way:

If we assume that `n` is not reached often, this approach would be simpler to implement, but generally, I would say this is the worse one, as when we are descended deep, we would benefit more from caching the deep directories.

#### b) Keeping `n` deepest directories

##### In cache:

The caching algorithm would make sure that it never keeps more open entries than `n`, and when it reaches `n`, to be able to be open a deeper layer, it closes the shallowest one it has.

##### In recursive implementation:

Recursion cannot handle this naturally, once many calls deep in recursion, the shallow file to be closed is far away in the stack.

##### Either way:

This never regresses compared to the current (one slot) cache: up to depth `n` it behaves exactly like the already-implemented unbounded stack, and past `n` it still never needs more reopens than the one slot cache would for the same sequence of calls, since it always keeps at least as much open as the one slot cache would, plus more.

When a lookup lands on a closed entry, reopening just that one directory (instead of the whole closed prefix leading to it) looks clumsy, but populating more of the prefix would only spend window capacity on directories we don't know we'll revisit, right before a redescent that, on a reasonably uniform tree, is likely to need most of that capacity itself. Reopening only what's needed keeps the rest of the window free for whatever comes next, instead of betting on an access pattern we can't predict.

## Conclusion

Inefficiency of using `fs.WalkDir` is the primary bottleneck, rather than the limitations of the one slot cache.

The cache avoids repeated `openat` walking and reopening of roots, independent of which walker uses it. Separately, even though the recursive implementation ended up giving a bigger improvement than the cache alone did, that doesn't make the cache skippable: a proper recursive implementation needs something like it anyway, to bound file descriptor usage against very deep paths, since plain recursion ties handle lifetime to call-stack depth and can't enforce a bound on its own.

After using both the recursive implementation and the limited multi-slot caching, the performance improvement is about 37%, reaching only 1.12 times slower than without using `os.Root`. This number will go down once the walk passes whatever file descriptor limit we settle on, since the cache then has to fall back to re-resolving some ancestors.

But this was demonstrated on directory-heavy data. In the original benchmark, the difference would be negligible.

> #### Profiling with `pprof`
> `Cached`:
> 
> ```
> 3.08s 76.62%  io/fs.WalkDir
> 2.12s 52.74%  io/fs.ReadDir
> 0.94s 23.38% go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.BenchmarkCached.func1
> 0.14s 3.48%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.(*Cache).RootForDir
> ```
 
…
> `StepByStepWalk`:
> 
> ```
> 2.22s 68.94%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.rootedWalkDirFn
> 1.02s 31.68%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.rootedWalkDirFn.func1
> 1.01s 31.37%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.BenchmarkStepByStepWalk.func1
> 0.13s  4.04%  go.podman.io/storage/internal/rootlookupcache.(*Cache).RootForDir
> ```
> 
> For this directory-heavy benchmark, I would say it looks like the primary bottleneck is the inefficient implementation of `ReadDir` rather than the limitations of the current cache or the inability to get the handle directly from `fs.WalkDir`.

The way I read this is that `os.rootFS.ReadDir` and `rootedWalkDirFn.func1` are basically exactly the same code: they differ in primarily in how they are called, where `fs.WalkDir` operates on the whole path in `fs.ReadDir` (= calls `openat` for each subdirectory in the path), while `rootedWalkDirFn` operates on the basename only. So I think _that’s_ the source of the difference.

---

> Inefficiency of using fs.WalkDir is the primary bottleneck, rather than the limitations of the one slot cache.

Thanks, the data is definitely a food for thought.

IIRC from earlier benchmarks, the cache/step-by-step implementations have quite a bit of extra memory allocations and cost of string operations, compared to NoRoot. It’s possible that a more integrated walk+cache could avoid a fair bit of that.

But at 1.12x cost of the unsafe implementation, we are probably close to the point of diminishing returns.
